title: Head-versus-tail choice at a planarian cut cannot be made locally

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Head-versus-tail choice at a planarian cut cannot be made locally

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When a planarian is cut once, cells that were adjacent neighbours at the same positional-information value make a head on one side and a tail on the other, so this anatomical decision cannot be made locally: wound cells must coordinate with the rest of the fragment to learn where they are, which way they face and what structures remain.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Left/right, head/tail: random, but collective anatomical decisions

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In other words, it is actually impossible for an anatomical decision like this to be made locally – the cells of the wound must coordinate with the remaining fragment to get information about where they are located, which way they are facing, and what other structures exist121,122, in order to make adaptive decisions about large-scale growth and form that enable regeneration of normal worms.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: McMillen P, Levin M, “Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates”, Communications biology (2024), doi:10.1038/s42003-024-06037-4; section “Introduction › Left/right, head/tail: random, but collective anatomical decisions”. Scope: Regenerating planarian fragments

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2024-collective-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing spatial expression and regeneration data can compare local and fragment-scale predictors. They cannot prove that every possible local mechanism is impossible, so only the need for known long-range information is partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Model head-versus-tail fate from strictly local wound measurements and test whether adding fragment-scale position, orientation, and remaining anatomy materially improves out-of-sample prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The word impossible is stronger than failure of current local models.

Local molecular states may already encode nonlocal history.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Head-versus-tail regeneration after one cut is among the most repeated observations in planarian biology, and very short or disrupted fragments are also widely reported. Those results live in many papers, while PlanMine holds markers rather than the cut outcomes. Opposite organs at one wound are real data, and they do not yet rule out local differences between the two faces, so the impossibility claim is only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: At a single planarian cut, record anterior-facing versus posterior-facing wound outcomes, and compare very short fragments or face-isolated tissue with fragments that retain long-range tissue. Opposite head and tail from one cut, lost when the fragment cannot communicate along its length, would support a non-local decision; correct polarity in an isolated wound face, or pre-existing molecular differences between the two faces, would allow a local account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The two wound faces are not the same cells; local planar polarity can differ across a cut.

Correct polarity does not show that wound cells learn position in any sense beyond receiving a cue.

Short-fragment and double-head results are scattered across papers rather than one outcome table.

fields.value:
